newsitem.title: USA: Ukraine president hears criticism of conditions.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine president hears criticism of conditions.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma heard criticism of crime and corruption in his country on Thursday as he met with political, business and financial leaders to reassure them about government and market reforms.

Sen. William Roth, chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, said after meeting with Kuchma that it was "critically important that Kiev clamp down on crime and corruption, which is growing at an alarming rate and is undermining international business interests in that nation."

If the problem persists, the Delaware Republican said, "it will undermine Western economic and political assistance programmes and the efforts of Western business to establish mutually beneficial relations with Ukraine."

Senior U.S. administration officials said however they were "very encouraged at the way things have been going" in the former Soviet state. The best way to root out corruption, they said, is for the country to make government more streamlined and transparent.
The country has suffered a number of "disappointing losses" in companies that scrapped plans for investment, they said, but Kuchma made that problem a priority and that was a sign of hope.

Kuchma met with a number of members of the U.S. Congress. His agenda also included talks with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michael Camdessus, World Bank President James Wolfensohn and a group of U.S. corporate chief executive officers.
Roth said another focus of his meeting was the need to insure the security of countries like Ukraine as NATO moves into its new relationship with Russia.

On Friday, Kuchma and U.S. Vice President Al Gore will preside at the first meeting of the Ukraine-U.S. Bi-national Commission, a coperative body which they co-chair. Kuchma was also scheduled to meet with President Bill Clinton.

Discussions in the new commission "will help us to renew trust between our two nations and boost development," Roman Shpek, head of Ukraine's National Agency for Reconstruction and Development, told a news conference.
Kuchma wants to make it clear his country "is faithful to the course of economic reforms" and restore trust in that process, Shpek added.
He said initial talks have taken place in an atmosphere where the parties were "friends and partners."

Ukraine was due to receive $330 million in U.S. grants and $650 million in loans during 1997. But the country has been criticised in the West for alleged widespread corruption, an unstable investment climate and mountains of red tape.

Last month the Group of Seven industrialised countries said it was "increasingly concerned that the Ukrainian government has been unable to implement the ambitious reform agenda developed in cooperation with the International Monetary Fund."

Shpek said he met with Representative Sonny Callahan, an Alabama Republican and a critic of Ukrainian steel sales in the United States, who said he would oppose further assistance unless the steel dumping issue is resolved.
He said the matter was being discussed and "we believe we will be able to come to a solution."

He also said a number of companies, including Boeing, Cargill, General Electric, Siemens and Royal Dutch Shell have agreed to serve on an advisory committee that will consult with Kuchma on the problems faced by foreign firms trying to do business in Ukraine.
